evidence.label: Elliptic capacity propagation and Fourier restriction to the sphere
Diagonal Fourier extension for positively curved surfaces in three dimensions

headline: Claimed proofs of the full Fourier restriction range p > 3 for the sphere and for positively curved surfaces.
scope: The claims are in three dimensions only, for compact smooth surfaces that curve the same way in every direction.
plain: Fourier extension builds a wave pattern in space by adding up waves whose frequencies lie on a curved surface. The restriction conjecture asks which size measures, called Lᵖ norms, keep that pattern finite. For curved surfaces in three dimensions the conjectured answer is every p above 3. One paper claims this for the sphere with bounded input. A second claims the matching Lᵖ-to-Lᵖ form for every compact positively curved surface.
doesNot: This does not settle the restriction conjecture in four or more dimensions, or the endpoint p = 3.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Peter Tomas, L² restriction theorem (with Stein)
scorecard.significanceWhy: Restriction in three dimensions is a central open problem in harmonic analysis, and these papers claim its full conjectured range.

explanation:
Start with the unit sphere in three-dimensional space and the constant function 1 on it. At each point x of space, add up the waves e^(2πi x·ω) over all points ω of the sphere. The total, called the extension E1(x), has an exact formula: 2 sin(2π|x|)/|x|. At x = 0 it equals 4π, about 12.57, the sphere's area. At distance 1/4 it equals 8. Far away it shrinks like 2/|x|.

Now measure its size with an Lᵖ norm: integrate |E1|ᵖ over all of space. For p = 3, each shell from radius R to 2R adds about the same amount. That amount is (128/3) × ln 2, about 29.57. Numerical integration gives 29.57 for R = 10, 20 and 40. Infinitely many shells make the total infinite. For p = 4 the shell totals halve at each doubling: about 3.77, 1.88 and 0.94. So that total is finite. The paper notes the integral diverges for every p up to 3[2].

The Fourier extension operator does the same for any function f on a surface. It weights each wave by the value of f. The restriction problem asks for which p this output has finite Lᵖ size, bounded by the size of f. In the bounded-data form, f is measured by its largest value. In the diagonal form, f is measured by the same Lᵖ norm on the surface. For surfaces that curve the same way in every direction, the conjectured range is every p above 3. The sphere example shows that p = 3 itself fails.

Elias Stein started the problem. The Tomas–Stein theory gives the classical bound from L² data to L⁴[3]. Bourgain tied restriction to the geometry of thin tubes. A wave packet is a piece of the output concentrated along such a tube. Curvature separates packet directions, but many tubes can still pass through a small region[4]. In 2016, Guth's polynomial partitioning reached bounded data for p > 13/4, which is 3.25[5]. Wang and Wu reached the diagonal bound for p > 22/7, about 3.143[6].

The sphere paper claims the full bounded-data range p > 3 for the sphere[1]. The second paper claims the diagonal bound for every p > 3[7]. It covers every compact smooth positively curved surface, including ones with a smooth edge. That includes the sphere, pieces of the elliptic paraboloid and smooth elliptic graphs[8]. Positive curvature means the surface bends the same way in every direction, like part of a ball.

The diagonal proof uses two theorem inputs[9]. One is the packet propagation theorem from the sphere paper. The other is a Kakeya maximal theorem from another paper in the same release[10]. It limits how weighted tubes pile up. The second paper also gives a consequence for the free Schrödinger equation in two space dimensions. It claims local smoothing for every p > 3 above Sobolev order 2 − 6/p[11]. A necessary condition of Rogers shows that this order cannot be lowered[12].

How sure is this? There is no Lean scope note for either paper, so no computer proof checker has tested them. The diagonal result depends on the sphere paper and on a Kakeya paper from the same release. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark if the papers hold, since they claim a central conjecture in three dimensions. They have no Lean scope note and depend on another unreviewed paper from the same release. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Building a function on space by adding up waves whose frequencies lie on a surface, each weighted by a given function.
A measure of a function's size: the p-th root of the integral of its absolute value to the power p.
The form of the problem where the input function is measured by its largest value.
A bound where input and output are measured with the same exponent p.
A piece of a wave pattern concentrated along a thin tube in one direction.
A surface that bends the same way in every direction at every point, like part of a ball.
A gain in smoothness for a wave or Schrödinger solution when averaged over a short time interval.
